item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.3.0: One-Click Xiaomi Camera Integration, Recordings Never Lost
item.description:
Got Xiaomi cameras at home? Want to keep your recordings on your own storage instead of relying on the cloud?

As someone with several Xiaomi cameras at home, I always had one frustration: every time I wanted to check the footage from my doorbell camera, I had to log into Xiaomi Cloud, wait for ages while it loaded, and it would often just spin. Plus, cloud storage charges by the day — it adds up over the month. And if you swap cameras, all your old recordings are gone. Pretty frustrating.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.4.0: Audio Recording Finally Arrives, Auto-Recovery When Cameras Go Down
item.description:

item.title: MiBeeHive: The "Hive" Toolbox I Built for My Studio
item.description: Coming from an operations background, later transitioning to development, the number of projects I maintain keeps growing. Various middleware, databases, monitoring components… each version upgrade is a manual labor: go to the official site to find the download link, compare version numbers, manually download to the internal network, then distribute to each machine. I used to write a bunch of Shell scripts to periodically pull the latest versions to the LAN — functional but not user-friendly: scripts scattered everywhere, adding new software required writing parsing logic by hand, and there was nothing to check when things went wrong.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.5.0: Full ONVIF Protocol Support + Hardware Transcoding + rpi-cam Co-development
item.description:
Less than a week after v0.4.0, v0.5.0 is a feature-dense release: full ONVIF protocol support (covering all five major services: Device/Media/PTZ/Imaging/Event), hardware transcoding (H.265 → H.264), and recorder reconnection optimizations. See the full changelog at GitHub Release Notes.

If you haven’t seen the previous versions, check out MiBeeNvr Introduction and v0.4.0 Technical Post.

Full ONVIF Protocol Support

v0.4.0 already had ONVIF device discovery and stream URL retrieval, but that was just the tip of the ONVIF iceberg. v0.5.0 completes the core services of ONVIF Profile S:

item.title: MiBeeSteward: Why I Built Another Device Management Tool in Go
item.description:
As a studio operator, the biggest pain point is never a specific problem — it’s the “not knowing” when devices multiply.

Not knowing which devices are alive, what services are running on them, whether a new machine has appeared on the network, whether a certain port is still open. This accumulated “not knowing” eventually becomes an outage.

My previous approach was a patchwork: Zabbix for monitoring, Nmap for scanning, Excel for asset tracking, Prometheus for metrics. Each tool is fine on its own, but together they’re a disaster — data silos, duplicate configuration, version drift, complex deployment.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.6.0: Timelapse + Transcoding UI + ONVIF Enhancements + Documentation Restructure
item.description: Once recording is up and running, storage becomes the first bottleneck. A single 1080p camera writes tens of GB per day — with a 30-day retention policy, a 1TB drive is mostly consumed. Many community members reported the same issue, and during discussions, the ideas of timelapse and transcoding storage gained the most traction: most of the time the scene is static, and compressing it with timelapse requires only 5% of the space for the same duration.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.6.0's Test Machines: Three Camera Projects Updated in Sync
item.description: The concurrently released MiBeeNvr v0.6.0 brought major features like timelapse, video transcoding, and ONVIF enhancements. Unit tests alone are far from enough — the full workflow must be tested against real camera hardware. To provide reliable test machines for this release, three camera projects were updated on the same day, June 5th — both to supply testing environments for the NVR and to solve some typical embedded development engineering problems along the way.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.7.0: Timelapse v2 + Dual-Lens Xiaomi + H.265 Muxing + Release Hardening
item.description: After v0.6.0 put the timelapse pipeline in place, community feedback quickly pointed out several hard problems: the JPEG sequence consumed too much storage, H.265 cameras couldn’t generate playable timelapse segments, dual-lens Xiaomi devices could only capture the main lens, and H.265 HLS would occasionally panic outright. None of these are edge cases — the dual-lens CW500 and Outdoor Cam 4 ship in large volumes in China, and H.265 is the de facto standard for mid-to-high-end cameras. The v0.7.0 mainline was built around exactly this feedback.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.2.0: Distributed Discovery + Change Detection + Topology + Fingerprint Library
item.description:
When v0.1.0 shipped, I wrote that it answers three questions: what devices are on the network, what they are, and how they relate. Honestly, v0.1.0 only answered the first half well — and only for the one LAN the center sat on.

The real-world layout is messier: one subnet in the office, one in the server room, another at home for test machines. The center lives in the office and literally cannot see the cameras in the server room. Getting it to scan the server room means crossing subnets — either opening up SNMP routing or just moving the center over there. Neither is elegant.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.9.0 → v0.9.1: ONVIF Zero-Config Auto-Discovery + Storage Rewrite + Lock-Free Camera Manager + Optional FFmpeg + Full i18n Repair
item.description: Nine cameras were hanging off a Banana Pi M5, and a few pieces of engineering debt had reached the point where they needed paying off. The /api/cameras endpoint would stall for 14.9 seconds while all 9 recorders started up — not because the traversal was slow, but because the cm.mu RWMutex was blocking, holding every read operation out. ONVIF camera addition still required typing in IP addresses manually, and with a household of CW500s, DS-2CD2047G2s, and others, every new camera meant opening a terminal session — not sustainable. FFmpeg as the only third-party binary dependency meant every deployment needed a check for whether it was installed, and on Raspberry Pi you also had to worry about hardware encoder compatibility. And the older Xiaomi devices — Dafang, Xiaofang, Aqara G2 — couldn’t be integrated at all because they speak the TUTK protocol. None of these are new technical challenges; they’re engineering debt, and v0.9 pays it off in one shot.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.3.0: Full L2 Topology + TLS Certificate Inventory + Container Images
item.description:
Take over an unfamiliar LAN and the first thing you need is to figure out what’s on it — office, server room, and home subnets tangled together, no documentation left behind, a switch full of MACs nobody can name. MiBeeSteward exists for exactly that: scan the network and tell you what devices are there, what they are, and how they connect.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.10.0-preview.1: End-to-End H.265 + Timelapse v3 + Auth Modernization + Architecture Cleanup (Paving the Way for Sidecar AI)
item.description:
v0.10.0-preview.1 is MiBeeNvr’s largest release since 0.8.0. The theme isn’t “add features”, it’s clean up the foundation: end-to-end H.265, Timelapse rewritten to v3, low-latency MJPEG, modernized auth, and a sweep of architecture cleanup across config / DI root / API routing / frontend player.

Why this much refactor at this point? After v0.9 paid off the accumulated engineering debt, the NVR’s mainline is heading in two directions — stronger AI capabilities, and support for more cameras. Both require a main process with clear internal structure, pluggable protocols, and AI inference that doesn’t block the video pipeline. The trade-offs discussed in the earlier research posts (frontend codec selection, streaming protocol landscape, NVR remote-access P2P survey, storage media selection) start landing in this release. A dedicated section at the end explains how this cleanup ties into the sidecar AI roadmap.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.10.1 → v0.11.0: fnOS Install Fixes + GB/T 28181 Support + Full-Day Playback Timeline
item.description: A few days after v0.10.0 went stable, fnOS users’ feedback boiled down to one sentence: it won’t install. It took seven rounds of installs on a live RK3582 fnOS box, plus SSH-ing into containers to read logs, to dig the three blockers out one by one. The previous release post here was still on v0.10.0-preview.1; that’s three versions unaccounted for — stable, patch, and now v0.11.0 — so this post covers them together.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.4.0: Router-Resident Discovery + OpenWrt Deployment + Device-Persistence Rewrite
item.description:
When v0.3.0 shipped container images, there was a non-negotiable precondition: the container had to run with --network host to see the full ARP table, otherwise MAC discovery dropped to zero. The root cause was the network namespace — the container couldn’t see the host’s /proc/net/arp packed with 30 rows.

v0.4.0 pushes that constraint to its logical conclusion: what if the discovery program runs on the gateway itself? The gateway is the choke point for all LAN traffic. DHCP leases, the conntrack connection table, hostapd’s wireless clients, dnsmasq’s DNS query log — this data is right there, no need to SNMP-poll a switch, no port scanning, zero extra network traffic. This release lets the center or agent reside directly on the router and taps these four passive sources.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.5.0: SNMPv3 + Multi-Role RBAC + Device Config Backup
item.description: Across the four releases from v0.1.0 to v0.4.0, MiBeeSteward assembled a complete internal-network device-management pipeline: active scanning and fingerprint identification handle discovery and classification; the agent and passive sources introduced in v0.2.0 (SNMP ARP, mDNS/SSDP multicast listening) extended discovery across multiple LANs, and v0.4.0 went further by letting the center and agent reside on the router, reading DHCP leases, conntrack, hostapd clients, and DNS query logs directly; heartbeat probing maintains online status while change detection emits device-added/changed/lost events; LLDP, CDP, and Bridge-MIB data feeds the L2 topology; TLS certificates of internal HTTPS services are collected as well. Deployment targets cover physical machines, VMs, containers, and OpenWrt routers.

item.title: Taking Over onvif-go: Real-Camera Fixes, Zero Dependencies, and Service Facades
item.description:
MiBeeNvr talks to cameras over ONVIF, and this library is what sits underneath. ONVIF is the de facto standard for IP video surveillance equipment: device discovery, media profiles, PTZ control, event subscriptions — all one set of SOAP-over-HTTP service conventions. Any brand that claims ONVIF compliance can, in theory, be integrated through the same calls.

onvif-go is that stack implemented in Go. We did not write it from scratch: its upstream was 0x524a/onvif-go — the previous author reshaped it into its modern form of a client plus a virtual camera server (the git history still traces back to earlier Go ONVIF attempts in the community). But upstream stalled entering 2026: the last merged PR landed in mid-January, the v1.0-through-v1.1.3 release cadence from late 2025 never resumed, and three Improve Test Coverage issues filed in November 2025 sit unclaimed to this day. Meanwhile we hit two problems in our own camera pool that could only be fixed inside the library.

item.title: Four Protocol Libraries, Extracted: ONVIF and GB28181 in Go and Rust
item.description:
MiBee’s camera access runs on two protocols. ONVIF is the de facto standard internationally — Hikvision, Axis, Dahua, and Bosch all speak it. GB/T 28181 is China’s national surveillance standard, unavoidable in government and state-owned projects. The device side (Raspberry Pi camera firmware, one Go and one Rust implementation) and the NVR side (MiBeeNvr, Go) both speak these two protocols, and the stacks have always lived inside the projects.

Two problems with that. First, this code is pickled in interop details — digest-auth qop handling, SIP Via-branch uniqueness, MANSCDP element-vs-attribute dual forms, TCP framing header byte counts — each one was ground out against a real platform, and a new project would have to grind them all again. Second, a library survey two weeks ago showed the open-source landscape for these protocols is unevenly populated; several positions have no one standing in them.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.12.0: Sub-streams, Adaptive Recording, and Full-path Observability
item.description:
MiBeeNvr v0.12.0 is out. This release goes after two everyday annoyances: watching the cameras on a phone, where a thumbnail-sized preview quietly pulls the full-resolution video underneath — eating data and heating the phone; and corridor or doorway cameras writing tens of GB a day that nobody ever replays.

Less disk

  • When nothing moves, the camera records less; the moment anything moves, it snaps back to full recording without dropping a frame. Quiet scenes measured at roughly 3/4 less disk
  • A louder sound, a doorbell, or a sensor signal also kicks it back to full recording
  • The replay timeline carries a green-to-red heat strip — the segments where something happened are visible at a glance
  • When the disk nears full, the quietest recordings are deleted first
  • Phone viewing defaults to a small, smooth stream: no stutter, no heat; one tap switches to HD for detail
  • When nobody is watching, that preview stream disconnects by itself — no camera connection or bandwidth tied up
